english: The chili pepper is really spicy.
tip: 진짜 (jinjja = really) — the casual-but-polite cousin of 정말 (jeongmal).
The word after 너무 (neomu) sets the tone: with 짜요 (jjayo = salty) it's a genuine 'too salty' complaint; before praise it would just mean 'so'.

english: The broth really hits the spot!
tip: 시원해요 (siwonhaeyo = refreshing) — Koreans say it even about hot soup that hits the spot.
뜨거워요 (tteugeowoyo) = hot to the touch; spicy-hot is 매워요 (maewoyo).
맛없어요 (madeopseoyo = tastes bad) — 맛 (taste) + 없다 (to not exist).

english: The chicken is nice and crispy.
tip: 치킨 (chikin) means fried chicken only; a live or raw chicken is 닭 (dak).

english: The taste is a little different.
tip: One letter apart: 달라요 (dallayo) = different, 달아요 (darayo) = sweet. 맛이 조금 달라요 (masi jogeum dallayo) = the taste is a bit different, not a bit sweet.
Korean has no verb "to need" – 필요 없어요 (piryo eopseoyo) is literally "necessity doesn't exist." To need something: 필요해요 (piryohaeyo).
배불러요 (baebulleoyo = I'm full) — 배 (belly) + 부르다; say it after a good meal.

english: I ordered pizza on the app.
tip: 에서 (eseo) marks where an action happens: 앱에서 (aebeseo = on the app) pairs with 주문했어요 (jumunhaesseoyo = ordered). Plain 에 (e) is just location, no action.
그릇 (geureut = bowl) with native numbers: 두 그릇 (du geureut = two bowls).

english: How much is the delivery fee?
tip: 비 (bi) on the end of a noun = fee: 배달비 (baedalbi = delivery fee).
Money uses Sino numbers: 삼천 원 (samcheon won = 3,000 won).

english: I drank every last drop of the broth.
tip: 까지 (kkaji) stretches from 'up to' into 'even': 국물까지 (gungmulkkaji) = even the broth – all the way down the list to the last thing.
돼요? (dwaeyo? = does it work?) is the all-purpose 'can I / do you take': 카드 돼요? (kadeu dwaeyo?) covers 'do you take cards?' in two words.
돼요 (dwaeyo) is the all-purpose "it works / it's fine": 카드 돼요 (kadeu dwaeyo) = cards are accepted. Noun + 돼요? asks if anything is possible.

english: How much did it come to?
tip: Bills "come out" in Korean: 얼마 나왔어요? (eolma nawasseoyo = how much is it?)
만 (man = 10,000) is the money unit: 사만 원 (saman won = 40,000 won).
The -(으)ㄹ게요 (-lgeyo) ending offers an action to the listener: 제가 계산할게요 (jega gyesanhalgeyo) = I'll get the bill – a volunteer move, not a prediction.
The -ㄹ게요 (-lgeyo) ending is a promise to the listener: 살게요 (salgeyo) = "I'll buy – I've got this." Plain 살 거예요 (sal geoyeyo) just states a plan.
씨 (ssi) after a name is the polite default – 민수 씨 (Minsu ssi). It follows the given name, and you never attach it to your own.
괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo) politely declines — a soft "no thanks."

english: Yesterday the company paid for dinner.
tip: 값 (gap = cost) attaches to nouns: 저녁값 (jeonyeokgap = the dinner bill).
Double consonant matters: 쌌어요 (ssasseoyo) = was cheap, 샀어요 (sasseoyo) = bought. 싸다 (ssada = cheap) vs 사다 (sada = buy).

english: We had a company dinner yesterday.
tip: 회식 (hoesik = team dinner) — after-work meals are big in Korean work life.

english: We grilled meat at the company dinner.
tip: 고기를 구웠어요 (gogireul guwosseoyo = grilled meat) – at a Korean barbecue the grill is set into your table and you cook the meat yourselves.

english: Do you take the subway to work?
tip: 로 (ro = by) marks transport: 지하철로 (jihacheollo = by subway).

english: Yes, I ride the subway every day.
tip: You ride the subway as a direct object: 지하철을 타요 (jihacheoreul tayo). 타다 (tada = ride) takes 을/를 – no 'on' or 'in'.
몇 (myeot) + a counter asks 'which number': 몇 호선 (myeot hoseon) = 'what number line?'. The same 몇 also asks 'how many'.

english: I get off at City Hall Station.
tip: Getting off happens AT a place, so it takes 에서: 시청역에서 내려요 (sicheongyeogeseo naeryeoyo). 에서 marks where an action happens – plain 에 won't work here.
